final_message:
The First Radish

I have been waiting for this day with the patience of a man who has nothing else to do, which is to say, not much patience at all. Every morning for three weeks I have gone out in my slippers to look at the radish-bed, and every morning the radish-bed has looked back at me with perfect composure, as if to say that a thing watched is a thing postponed. Polly says I am wearing a path. I tell her it is a path of devotion, and she says it is a path to the doctor, if I catch cold.

But this morning, behold! Six little red shoulders pushing up out of the earth, round and shining, like so many aldermen at a public dinner. I pulled one. It came out with a sound I can only describe as modest, and I stood there holding it, with the dirt falling off my fingers, quite unable to say anything. There is a moment in a man's life, between the pulling and the eating, when he is the richest person in the county. I recommend it.

I washed it at the pump. I did not take it into the house, because the house has opinions about such things, and I wanted none of them. I ate it standing in the garden, with the dew still on the leaves, and I must report that it was hot, sharp, and entirely satisfactory. It tasted of spring, and of money saved, and a little of the pump. The neighbors' hens watched me through the fence with what I took to be envy. I gave them the tops, which they accepted without gratitude.

It is a curious fact that the first vegetable of the year is always the best, whatever it may be. I have had radishes in July that would shame a turnip; but they were merely radishes. This one was a victory. It had survived the late frost, the cutworm, and my own advice to it. I think of all the lettuce and beans and cucumbers that are to follow, and how I shall presently be giving them away to people who do not want them, and hiding when they come to the door; but that is a trouble for another season. Today there is only the radish, and the sun, and a man in slippers, quite content.

Polly has asked what we are to have for dinner. I have told her: five radishes, and a great deal of salt.
